28: [enforce prohibitions outside the agent](architecture-heuristics.md#enforce-prohibitions-outside-the-agent),
29: and that applies here: an agent that never opens this document still produces
30: documentation. A mechanical check is the boundary, and this rule is what that
31: check enforces.
32: 
33: ## The Rule
34: 
35: An authoritative document describes what the system does, in present tense, as
36: a contract. It is not a changelog.
37: 
38: Git history and the issue tracker already record how the system reached its
39: current behavior, losslessly and with better tooling. Restating that history in
40: prose adds length without adding recoverable information, and it makes the
41: documentation grow with the number of issues handled rather than with the
42: number of contracts the system has.
43: 
44: ## The Rebuild Bar
45: 
46: An authoritative document describes current behavior in enough detail to rebuild
47: that behavior without reading the implementation. A reader who has to open the
48: code to learn what the contract is has found a gap in the document.
49: 
50: This is the bar the documentation aims at, not a claim that prose regenerates a
51: schema byte for byte. What a rebuild needs is the shape of the contract: the
52: fields and their meaning, the limits, the states and the transitions between
53: them, the ordering guarantees, the failure classes, and the conditions that
54: select between behaviors. The particular expression that implements them is not
55: part of the contract and does not belong in the document.
56: 
57: The bar bounds `The Rule` above and `The Delete-The-Issue-Number Test` below.
58: That rule removes narrative, and nothing in it opposes removing more than
59: narrative; a document can satisfy every rule of form and still have lost
60: something a reader needs. The bar is that opposition. It is the limit on how far
61: tightening may go.
62: 
63: It is stated here, ahead of the procedure that removes text, so that a reader
64: working through this document in order meets the limit before the licence.
65: 
66: ## Completeness Against Concision
67: 
68: The set grows without bound when every change adds a paragraph keyed to itself,
69: and the rebuild bar requires each document to be complete. These pull in
70: opposite directions on volume. The resolution is fixed here rather than struck
71: again in each document:
72: 
73: - Narrative about how the system came to behave this way is always removable.
74: - A statement of what the system does is removable only when it is duplicated,
75:   covered by a linked document that owns it, or wrong.
76: 
77: Length is never by itself a reason to remove a statement of behavior. A document
78: that is long because it states many contracts is the right length. A document
79: that is long because it recounts the changes that produced those contracts is
80: not, and the rule above already removes that.
81: 
82: The three grounds are narrower than they read. *Duplicated* means the same
83: contract is stated twice in the same document, not that two documents each state
84: a contract about the same subsystem. *Covered by a linked document that owns it*
85: means the linked document carries that statement, which is checkable by opening
86: it; replacing a statement with a link to a document that does not carry it loses
87: the statement. *Wrong* is not a licence to delete during a rewrite: a statement
88: found inaccurate against the implementation is recorded as separate work under
89: `Changing A Contract` below, so the correction is visible as a change to the
90: contract rather than as an absence.
91: 
92: ## The Delete-The-Issue-Number Test
93: 
94: This test removes text, and `The Rebuild Bar` above is the limit on what it may
95: remove. The test decides whether a sentence is narrative. A sentence stating what
96: the system does is not narrative however it is phrased, so it is outside what
97: this test may take, and `Completeness Against Concision` above gives the only
98: three grounds for removing one.
99: 
100: Apply this test to every sentence carrying an issue reference:
101: 
102: - Delete the issue number and read the sentence again.
103: - If it stays true and complete, the reference was decoration. Remove it.
104: - If it stops making sense, the sentence was changelog prose. Rewrite it as a
105:   statement of current behavior.
106: 
107: A worked pair from an earlier revision of `planner-research-handoff.md`, with
108: issue numbers anonymized:
109: 
110: > The trusted `repository_planner` tool requires `researchHandoff` on
111: > `plan.finalize`. Issue #NNN replaces the earlier expanded resource with a
112: > compact reference. Each reuse resource contains exactly three fields: …
113: 
114: The field list is true without the second sentence, so that sentence goes and
115: the fields stay. Contrast `automatic-plan-v1-handoff.md`:
116: 
117: > Issue #NNN does not replace this handoff. Automatic workflows enter it after
118: > the effective accepted Plan settles without an unresolved pre-handoff
119: > request. Planner-led workflows additionally require …
120: 
121: Deleting the number leaves the first sentence saying nothing: it is a reply to a
122: change a reader cannot see. The sentences after it already state how each
123: workflow mode enters the handoff, which is the behavior the first sentence was
124: reaching for, so the opener goes and the rest stays. Where no such statement
125: follows, write one instead of deleting the sentence.
126: 
127: ## Keep And Drop
128: 
129: Issue references are not banned. Three kinds are load-bearing and stay:
130: 
131: 1. **Decision records.** An architecture decision record, or an accepted owner
132:    decision in `architecture-heuristics.md`, records who decided what and when.
133:    A decision is inherently historical, so its date and its deciding issue are
134:    part of the record rather than decoration.
135: 2. **Run-specific verification provenance.** A claim whose only support is one
136:    identified run — a real-model smoke, a measured benchmark, a captured visual
137:    check — keeps the identity of that run: candidate commit or branch, date, and
138:    the issue that produced it. Without it a reader cannot tell what the claim
139:    covers or when it has gone stale.
140: 3. **Supersession notes.** A deliberate statement that an earlier documented
141:    behavior no longer applies, retained because readers and retained data still
142:    hold the earlier behavior. Keep such a note while a compatibility path,
143:    retained session, or stored record preserves the earlier behavior, and remove
144:    it when that path goes.
145: 
146: Everything else drops. A retained reference names a record; it does not narrate.
147: `Owner decision, accepted 2026-09-18` is the retained form. `Issue #NNN replaces
148: the earlier expanded resource` is not. Retaining a reference under the second or
149: third kind is a judgement, and `Recording A Retention` below says how to make that
150: judgement visible.
151: 
152: When a passage cannot be rewritten under this rule without losing information,
153: that is a defect in the rule. Report it against this document rather than
154: resolving it as a local exception.
155: 
156: ## Recording A Retention
157: 
158: A reference the rule retains by human judgement carries a marker on its paragraph,
159: so the judgement is visible to a reader and to the check that enforces this rule:
160: 
161: ```markdown
162: <!-- keep-issue-ref: supersession — retained while the pre-compact input path exists -->
163: Before #NNN, a missing durable title could be filled by a planner-supplied title.
164: ```
165: 
166: The category is `decision`, `verification-run`, or `supersession`, matching the three
167: retained kinds above, and the text after it says why this reference is load-bearing;
168: a marker without that reason retains nothing. The marker applies to the paragraph
169: containing it, but it never retains a narrative form: an issue-keyed heading, or a
170: reference opening a sentence as its subject, is dropped with or without a marker.
171: Write the retained reference so it names its record rather than narrating. The
172: marker is an HTML comment, so it does not render.
173: 
174: Two retained kinds need no marker, because their context already establishes them: every
175: reference in a document under `adr/`, and a reference in the paragraph of a dated
176: `Owner decision, accepted <date>` line.
177: 
178: ## Measuring
179: 
180: `npm run docs:references` reports issue-reference density per authoritative document,
181: ranked worst-first, with a repository total, and enforces the rule in this document.
182: 
183: ```bash
184: npm run docs:references                 # ranked table, repository total, enforcement
185: npm run docs:references -- --locations  # every reference with file:line:column
186: npm run docs:references -- --document docs/authoritative/owner-cli.md
187: npm run docs:references -- --compare    # movement against the recorded baseline
188: npm run docs:references -- --json       # the same report as JSON
189: ```
190: 
191: Each reference is reported as retained, drop, or needing judgement:
192: 
193: - **retained** is a reference the rule keeps without a reader: an `adr/` document, a dated
194:   owner decision, or an explicit keep marker.
195: - **drop** is a narrative form the rule names: an issue-keyed heading, or a reference
196:   opening a sentence as its subject.
197: - **needs judgement** is everything else. A reference inside a block quote or a code span
198:   is reported here as quoted material: a document showing `Issue #NNN replaces the
199:   earlier expanded resource` to illustrate the rule is neither narrating nor deciding,
200:   and the rule names no category for it.
201: 
202: Run-specific verification provenance and supersession notes are reported as needing
203: judgement rather than as retained. No pattern separates them from narrative prose without
204: reading the sentence: `Issue #NNN replaces the earlier expanded resource` and
205: `Before #NNN, a missing durable title could be filled in` share their vocabulary, and the
206: rule drops the first and keeps the second. Reporting them as retained would overstate how
207: clean the set is, which is worse than reporting nothing. Enforcement closes that gap the
208: only way it can: a reference reported as needing judgement fails the run until the rule
209: is applied to it, which turns it into prose with no reference or into a marked retention.
210: 
211: `.relayview/issue-reference-baseline.json` holds a fixed measurement that
212: `--compare` reports movement against, so progress is visible without re-deriving the
213: starting point. `--write-baseline` replaces it, which is a deliberate act that resets the
214: comparison: record a new baseline when the owner accepts a new starting point, not to
215: clear a regression.
216: 
217: ## Enforcement
218: 
219: The check enforces the keep/drop rule, not a count. A run fails when any
220: reference is a form the rule drops or one it cannot classify, and passes with

46: An authoritative document describes current behavior in enough detail to rebuild
47: that behavior without reading the implementation. A reader who has to open the
48: code to learn what the contract is has found a gap in the document.

51: schema byte for byte. What a rebuild needs is the shape of the contract: the
52: fields and their meaning, the limits, the states and the transitions between
53: them, the ordering guarantees, the failure classes, and the conditions that
54: select between behaviors. The particular expression that implements them is not
55: part of the contract and does not belong in the document.

57: The bar bounds `The Rule` above and `The Delete-The-Issue-Number Test` below.

97: this test may take, and `Completeness Against Concision` above gives the only
98: three grounds for removing one.

1: # Trusted Model-Provider Credential Delivery
2: 
3: <!-- keep-issue-ref: supersession — names the retained record of the pre-preset Z.ai setup -->
4: The superseded pre-preset setup used to verify the Z.ai binding is retained in
5: [Issue #301 stacked credential verification](../historical/verification/issue-301-stacked-credential-verification.md).
6: 
7: ## Implemented Boundary
8: 
9: Three provider bindings are admitted: OpenRouter, the Z.ai Global Coding Plan, and the local-Qwen binding. Each is a fixed non-secret identity; the roles that may receive each one are in the Process Scoping section below. The OpenRouter identity is:
10: 
11: - owner binding: `openrouter-api-key`;
12: - KeePassXC/systemd identity: `relayview-openrouter-api-key`;
13: - encrypted TPM2 artifact: `/etc/credstore.encrypted/aspect-relayview-openrouter-api-key.cred`;
14: - Pi-supported process variable: `OPENROUTER_API_KEY`.
15: 
16: The Z.ai identity is:
17: 
18: - owner binding: `zai-coding-api-key`;
19: - KeePassXC/systemd identity: `relayview-zai-coding-api-key`;
20: - encrypted TPM2 artifact: `/etc/credstore.encrypted/aspect-relayview-zai-coding-api-key.cred`;
21: - one-use foreground bootstrap: `RELAYVIEW_ZAI_CREDENTIAL_BOOTSTRAP`;
22: - Pi-supported process variable: `ZAI_API_KEY`.
23: 
24: The KeePassXC entry remains the operator-controlled source of truth. `keepassxc-credential` may create the TPM2-encrypted systemd artifact needed for unattended startup, but the repository, owner database, task/session records, browser, CLI/TUI requests, manifests, and profile files never contain the decrypted value. The binding name is accepted only in trusted owner configuration; tasks and agents cannot choose a credential identity, path, variable, or value.
25: 
26: An OpenRouter workflow profile must declare `providerCredential: openrouter-api-key` and literal `PI_PROVIDER=openrouter`. A Z.ai planner or implementer must declare `providerCredential: zai-coding-api-key` and exact literal identities `PI_PROVIDER=zai` and `PI_MODEL=glm-5.3`; its profile may contain only those literal provider/model assignments, so the built-in Global Coding Plan endpoint remains owner/runtime controlled. The referenced profiles reject `PI_SECRET_ENV_FILE`, API-key assignments, command substitutions, arbitrary endpoints, and arbitrary statements. The checked-in [Muse profile](../../config/examples/openrouter-muse-spark-1.3-contributor.env), [GLM-5.3 profile](../../config/examples/zai-glm-5.3-coding-plan.env), and [owner configuration](../../config/examples/owner-planner-research.yaml) are the supported templates. The permanent catalog carries the GLM profile, its planner, and a separate GLM implementer identity on that same credential binding.
27: 
28: The local binding is `qwen-api-key`, mapped only to
29: `relayview-qwen-api-key`, with TPM2 artifact
30: `/etc/credstore.encrypted/aspect-relayview-qwen-api-key.cred` and KeePassXC
31: entry `Automation/Qwen API`. Only owner-approved `local-vllm` roster entries may
32: select it, within their declared role eligibility. Their profiles contain literal non-secret routing and identity values;
33: API-key assignments and secret-file fallback are rejected. The Pi catalog must
34: use exactly `"apiKey": "${OPENAI_API_KEY}"`, with no provider headers or per-model
35: route/auth overrides. Pi gives a saved `local-vllm` credential in `auth.json`
36: precedence over that reference, so any such entry is rejected. Malformed auth
37: storage also fails closed; unrelated provider credentials are preserved. Both
38: prompt-free admission and every Qwen session launch/reopen check the selected
39: catalog/auth directory before credential delivery. The owner never deletes saved
40: authentication to make a launch pass. To resolve a conflict, open Pi, use `/logout`,
41: and select **Local vLLM** (the provider ID is `local-vllm`); this removes only the
42: saved provider credential, leaving the catalog and TPM enrollment intact. Restart
43: the owner afterward. The verified host currently has no conflicting entry.
44: 
45: ## Process Scoping
46: 
47: For an installed system owner, systemd decrypts each named credential into its private credential directory. Before every bound session launch, the owner invokes `keepassxc-credential assert-current` with only the binding's fixed non-secret identity, validates the exact delivered regular file, reads one bounded line, and gives Pi only that descriptor's provider variable. It also forces `PI_SECRET_ENV_FILE=/dev/null` so the installation wrapper cannot fall back to a plaintext profile secret file. Pi 0.85.0's admitted OpenRouter and Global Z.ai providers read `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` and `ZAI_API_KEY` respectively.
48: 
49: Owner decision, accepted 2026-10-02: **OpenRouter, Z.ai, and Qwen bindings are each eligible for the planner, Plan reviewer, and implementer roles.** The Z.ai exact `zai/glm-5.3` model gate remains a model constraint, not a role constraint. Per-model role eligibility is declared on each unified-roster entry's `providerCredential.eligibleRoles` (default all three roles); a role outside a model's declared eligibility cannot be selected, reserved, launched, reopened, or recovered with that credential and resolves with a sanitized typed unavailability. The supervisor admits each binding only on its exact provider and model: Z.ai only on exact `zai/glm-5.3`, Qwen only on `local-vllm`. Integrator, expert, legacy/arbitrary, provider-mismatched, and unrelated-model sessions cannot select these bindings, and launch specifications cannot supply `OPENROUTER_API_KEY`, `OPENAI_API_KEY`, `ZAI_API_KEY`, any credential bootstrap, or `PI_SECRET_ENV_FILE` themselves. The child environment starts from a narrow host allowlist; systemd's credential directory, provider keys, and other owner ambient state do not propagate. A bound Z.ai planner, implementer, or reviewer receives only `ZAI_API_KEY` plus `PI_SECRET_ENV_FILE=/dev/null`; the bound local planner, implementer, or reviewer receives only its Qwen value as `OPENAI_API_KEY`. Owner-mediated commands/validation, Git, naming, brokers, compatibility probes, and unrelated sessions receive neither provider values nor delivery handles. OpenAI Codex sessions remain OAuth-only and receive no API-key fallback.
50: 
51: A `same_as_planner` reviewer inherits the planner's fixed credential binding and provider/model assignment. An explicitly selected reviewer carries its own roster entry's binding within the declared role eligibility. Reviewer cloning itself remains offline; the eventual trusted reviewer Pi process receives the same scoped provider access. The pre-readiness reasoning metadata probe also remains offline and sends no prompt, but does not consume or expose the credential: it bypasses the credential-demanding installation profile wrapper with the profile's already-validated public credential-bound provider/model identities, then verifies the same identities in Pi's state response. Existing active processes retain the credential bytes they started with and are never silently reassigned.
52: 
53: Qwen uses the same boundary with `OPENAI_API_KEY`. Its model-accessible `read`,
54: `grep`, `find`, and `ls` tools use the existing [confined filesystem dispatcher](planner-filesystem-containment.md).
55: The planner's primary root is its immutable source workspace; the implementer's
56: primary root is its stored worktree. Either may use only assigned read-only
57: supporting roots. A new reviewer-v3 and any retained reviewer-v2 whose source
58: model profile still matches receive the current review round's exact candidate
59: worktree as their only root, while retained reviewer-v1 assignments have no
60: filesystem tools. Qwen reviewer-v1 and reviewer-v2 assignments fail closed
61: under the current checkpoint and model-profile lineage. Process environments, owner state, home authentication
62: files, and paths or symlinks outside those roots are denied. A missing filesystem
63: extension acknowledgment prevents readiness. Reopen/recovery reconstructs the
64: boundary; it does not reuse unrestricted native read tools. Existing implementer
65: role instructions and verified skill text are supplied through explicit trusted
66: prompts. Automatic context/template discovery is disabled; applicable repository
67: instructions must be read through confined tools. This also prevents symlinked
68: `AGENTS.md` or discovered system-prompt files from reading the credential-bearing
69: process environment during startup or recovery. Write/edit and restricted bash
70: behavior are preserved. Stop/restart existing Qwen sessions to apply this boundary
71: to processes already running the earlier PR candidate.
72: 
73: Its bootstrap variable is consumed and deleted, and ambient `QWEN38_API_KEY` is stripped. Provider-authored `errorMessage` diagnostics are replaced before supervisor events/history are projected; model-authored text remains model content.
74: 
75: The unavoidable boundary is process-level environment exposure: the trusted Pi provider process and same-UID operating-system inspection can observe its assigned `OPENROUTER_API_KEY`, `ZAI_API_KEY`, or `OPENAI_API_KEY`. RelayView does not claim containment stronger than the Linux process boundary or Pi's provider transport.
76: 
77: ## Foreground Development
78: 
79: Foreground development uses the helper's interactive `run-live` path and a dedicated one-use bootstrap variable. The helper asks KeePassXC to unlock through the terminal, exports the value only to the owner process, and executes the owner without placing either secret in argv or stdout:
80: 
81: ```zsh
82: keepassxc-credential run-live \
83:   --database /home/anodyine/KeePassXCVault/automation.kdbx \
84:   --entry 'Automation/OpenRouter API' \
85:   --env RELAYVIEW_OPENROUTER_CREDENTIAL_BOOTSTRAP \
86:   -- npm run owner:dev
87: ```
88: 
89: The owner captures and deletes that bootstrap and strips ambient `OPENROUTER_API_KEY`, `OPENAI_API_KEY`, and `PI_SECRET_ENV_FILE` before constructing command, validation, Git, or child-process boundaries. A simultaneous foreground Brave run may nest a second `run-live` using `RELAYVIEW_BRAVE_CREDENTIAL_BOOTSTRAP`; ordinary workflow-smoke deliberately rejects all ambient provider variables and uses only systemd enrollment.
90: 
91: For Qwen foreground delivery, use the same command with entry `Automation/Qwen API`
92: and bootstrap `RELAYVIEW_QWEN_CREDENTIAL_BOOTSTRAP`. Nested `run-live` calls
93: can deliver independent bindings. Never export the source `QWEN38_API_KEY`.
94: 
95: For Z.ai, use entry `Automation/Z.AI Coding Plan` and bootstrap
96: `RELAYVIEW_ZAI_CREDENTIAL_BOOTSTRAP`. The owner consumes and deletes that
97: bootstrap before constructing other process boundaries. Nested `run-live` calls
98: may carry Brave, OpenRouter, Z.ai, and Qwen independently; never export
99: `ZAI_API_KEY` in the calling shell.

101: ## Enrollment, Rotation, And Revocation
102: 
103: For OpenRouter, create the KeePassXC entry at `Automation/OpenRouter API`, save the database, then enroll:
104: 
105: ```zsh
106: keepassxc-credential probe --mode tpm2
107: keepassxc-credential enroll relayview-openrouter-api-key \
108:   --database /home/anodyine/KeePassXCVault/automation.kdbx \
109:   --entry 'Automation/OpenRouter API' \
110:   --mode tpm2
111: keepassxc-credential status relayview-openrouter-api-key
112: ```
113: 
114: The password and selected entry value are requested interactively and are never command arguments. A current enrollment reports `enrolled=yes`, `mode=tpm2`, and `current=yes`.
115: 
116: After changing the KeePassXC password field, save the database and run `rotate` with the same non-secret arguments. Restart the installed owner or workflow-smoke unit so systemd admits the new encrypted artifact. New sessions then use the rotated value; already-running Pi processes retain their original environment until explicitly stopped. `re-enroll` repairs the machine copy from the current vault entry. `remove relayview-openrouter-api-key` deletes only the machine-local encrypted enrollment and metadata, not the KeePassXC entry. Stop active OpenRouter sessions and restart the owner when revocation must take effect immediately.
117: 
118: `assert-current` fingerprints the synchronized KeePassXC database. A database edit after enrollment yields `stale_enrollment`; the owner never silently uses that binding for a new session. Exact command replay and concurrent launches read the same owner-approved binding and do not perform enrollment or write vault state.
119: 
120: For Qwen, substitute `relayview-qwen-api-key` and `Automation/Qwen API`
121: in these enrollment, rotation, status, re-enrollment and removal commands. Saving
122: any edit to this shared vault changes its fingerprint: re-enroll other stale
123: bindings after all edits are saved. Existing services must restart to load new
124: systemd-delivered bytes; running Pi processes retain their original bytes. Removing
125: the encrypted enrollment prevents future delivery; stop active sessions and restart
126: the owner for immediate revocation. No server API key is rotated by these commands.
127: 
128: For Z.ai, substitute `relayview-zai-coding-api-key` and
129: `Automation/Z.AI Coding Plan`. Saving any change to the shared database makes all
130: earlier enrollments stale, so finish the vault edits first and re-enroll every
131: binding that must remain current. Rotation, re-enrollment, removal, owner restart,
132: and active-process semantics are the same as OpenRouter. These commands do not
133: rotate or revoke the upstream Z.ai key itself.
134: 
135: ## Readiness And Failure Semantics
136: 
137: Credential readiness distinguishes `missing_enrollment`, `stale_enrollment`, `delivery_unavailable`, `credential_malformed`, `unsupported_launch_mechanism`, and `delivery_ready`. `delivery_ready` means only that the narrow launch boundary admitted the value; it is deliberately not provider readiness. A successful authenticated Pi turn advances the internal state to `ready`. Sanitized Pi error evidence distinguishes `provider_rejected`, `model_unavailable`, `provider_rate_limited`, and `provider_quota_exhausted` without retaining raw provider diagnostics or the key. A missing or failed optional Z.ai binding does not prevent independently usable OAuth, OpenRouter, Qwen, or Brave paths from becoming ready.
138: 
139: A missing optional OpenRouter binding does not prevent the owner, ChatGPT OAuth planner path, local implementer, or Brave broker from starting. API minor 16 maps credential readiness to a sanitized available/unavailable planner choice. A workflow that selects the unavailable OpenRouter preset fails before its prompt is admitted, without switching to GPT-5.6 Sol; after that observation, newly read forms expose the updated sanitized state.
140: 
141: The 2026-09-03 real Muse smoke verified successful TPM2 delivery and exact `openrouter` / `meta/muse-spark-1.3-contributor` selection. Its first request received provider HTTP `403` for the account's missing initial age attestation; after confirmation, routing returned `404` because the sole endpoint was excluded by the account's paid-model training policy. These are `provider_rejected` and `model_unavailable` outcomes respectively, not missing/stale delivery or invalid-key diagnoses. The account owner explicitly accepted both provider policies, after which the same credential completed an authenticated inference, one real read-only `read` tool call, and a settled answer without creating a plan or implementation. Account policy is changed only in OpenRouter, never by this owner. Rotating a current credential does not resolve either policy gate.
142: 
143: Provider-qualified model identities containing `/` remain projectable in the public schema instead of collapsing the snapshot to `owner_internal_error`. Recovery retains the exact model identity and shows the failed and successful turns without exposing the credential.
144: 
145: ## Qwen verification status
146: 
147: On 2026-09-07 the operator enrolled the Qwen entry with TPM2 and reported
148: `current=yes`. A transient systemd process on the RelayView host loaded only that
149: mapping and authenticated to `http://192.168.0.38:8899/v1/models`, which reported
150: `flash-next-w4a16` and the then-current `max_model_len: 131072`. Missing and deliberately incorrect
151: keys each returned HTTP 401. This establishes authenticated transport and those
152: rejection cases, not checkpoint identity, inference, tool compatibility, or the
153: full production workflow. On 2026-09-09 the same credential boundary authenticated
154: the reconfigured route at `max_model_len: 147456`; the 147456/32768 candidate
155: catalog's Pi tool/history check passed at the exact Flash identity and effort
156: `xhigh`. Owner-preset regressions separately verify planner/reviewer v2 and
157: implementer v4 lineage. On 2026-09-15 the unchanged binding authenticated the
158: replacement Intel AutoRound checkpoint at exact revision
159: `4c67bf686b7f7fd386bae6b07ab59e8ff1d5b897`; `/models` reported
160: `max_model_len: 122880`, a bounded tool call passed, and an authenticated
161: 32,768-token-cap request completed with retained reasoning. New
162: planner/reviewer/implementer assignments use v3/v3/v5. The production deletion
163: workflow, independent replay and owner restart passed for the prior admission.
164: Isolated encrypted-copy checks cover changed-value rejection, fresh TPM2
165: resealing/new-unit delivery, stale enrollment and removal while leaving the real
166: enrollment unchanged. Server-side key replacement was not performed; see
167: [Flash admission](qwen-flash-admission.md) for exact evidence and repeatable checks.
168: 
169: ## Installed Service And Workflow Smoke
170: 
171: `owner install-service --online-system` accepts the existing `--credential-file` Brave artifact and independent `--openrouter-credential-file`, `--zai-credential-file`, and `--qwen-credential-file` artifacts. Each adds exactly one fixed `LoadCredentialEncrypted=` mapping. Provider-only system services need no Brave credential or wrapper; all four mappings can coexist. The Brave wrapper continues to bootstrap research; the owner consumes each separately named provider file only for its bound Pi process. Brave-only and credential-free user units retain their prior behavior.
172: 
173: `workflow-smoke start` selects its systemd boundary when any preset requests broker-only research, uses OpenRouter or Z.ai, or binds Qwen for either workflow role. It loads only the required mappings: provider-only runs do not launch the Brave wrapper or require Brave startup verification, while combined runs carry each independent mapping. Manifests retain encrypted artifact paths and identities but no decrypted value. The smoke rejects inherited Brave/OpenRouter/Z.ai/OpenAI keys, foreground bootstrap variables, and plaintext secret-file handles before building or launching anything.
174: 
175: ## ChatGPT OAuth availability
176: 
177: The Sol planner and reference implementer share the existing Pi-managed ChatGPT OAuth login. The owner does not enroll, refresh or export OAuth credentials and introduces no API-key fallback. The Qwen conflict check parses the shared auth store only to reject a saved `local-vllm` entry; it does not change any provider credentials. Profiles permit only literal `PI_PROVIDER` and `PI_MODEL` assignments. Owner admission remains prompt-free; before reservation and preset-backed runtime readiness, a bounded `pi auth check --provider openai-codex --json --no-refresh` checks local OAuth admission. The subprocess receives a small host-environment allowlist, a five-second timeout and an 8 KiB output ceiling. Only a fixed status vocabulary escapes this boundary; stderr and extra JSON fields are discarded.
178: 
179: `subscription_admitted` means local OAuth admission, not verified expiry, account entitlement, quota, endpoint reachability, or successful inference. Pi 0.85.0's no-refresh check does not prove those facts. A final successful request establishes `provider_ready`; observed errors yield bounded missing/expired login, provider rejection, model unavailability, rate/quota limit, or generic request failure. Retry frames do not establish final availability. Both roles sharing that provider/model expose the same observed state. Runtime provider diagnostics in `errorMessage` fields are replaced before supervisor events/history are projected; model-authored content is not treated as a credential diagnostic.

This is deliberately not a quota poll or automatic retry. Local presets remain available; selected tasks never switch to them automatically. Catalog/profile drift, incompatible runtime, unsupported reasoning, and first-state provider/model/effort mismatches remain separate typed pre-prompt failures. 51: - `GET /health/ready`, which returns 200 only for `ready` and otherwise returns 503.

See [Shared Security, Protocol, Owner, And Test Primitives](shared-security-protocol-and-test-primitives.md). Persisted nonterminal sessions then become `recovering`, process attempts become unverified, and interrupted barriers remain closed. For every other session, the application layer builds explicit reopen specifications from verified internal store records, coordinates supervisor results, and fences ambiguous accepted effects as recovery-required; the supervisor does not invent liveness or scan history on its own.
60: 
61: ## Session Ownership
62: 
63: Each live session has:
64: 
65: - one durable `sessionId` supplied by the caller;
66: - one monotonically increasing filesystem-fenced ownership generation;
67: - one unique ownership epoch;
68: - one process-attempt ID;
69: - the owner process identity;
70: - the child PID, Linux `/proc` start-time ticks, and boot ID;
71: - an atomic heartbeat timestamp.
72: 
73: The lease root is supplied by the owner runtime and belongs under its protected runtime directory. Session IDs are hashed before becoming lease paths. Claiming uses an atomic directory rename, so competing owners cannot both acquire one session. Generation metadata remains after normal release so a reopen receives a newer generation.
74: 
75: A live matching owner process always causes `ownership_conflict`; heartbeat age alone never authorizes takeover. When the recorded owner process is dead, the session is reported `orphaned`. A recorded child is signaled only after its PID, start time, and boot ID still match. Because inherited RPC stdio cannot be reattached, the new owner terminates that exact orphaned process group, reclaims the stale lease, enters `recovering`, and reopens verified history in a new process attempt. A PID or lock file alone is never sufficient evidence.
76: 
77: Commands require the current ownership generation. Stale callers receive `stale_owner_epoch`. 3: This document records accepted, cross-cutting decision guidance for RelayView.
4: Heuristics are defaults for evaluating new designs; they are neither domain
5: vocabulary nor claims that a behavior has been implemented. A design may depart
6: from a heuristic when it records the concrete invariant, limitation, or evidence
7: that requires the exception. A consequential, hard-to-reverse exception may
8: also require an architecture decision record.
9: 
10: Verified current behavior remains documented in the relevant authoritative
11: subsystem contract. Specific consequential decisions and their tradeoffs remain
12: documented in `docs/authoritative/adr/`. The form those documents take — present
13: tense, contract rather than changelog, and which issue references are retained —
14: is governed by [authoritative documentation standards](authoritative-documentation-standards.md),
15: not by a heuristic here. The accepted owner decisions below are one of the
16: reference categories that document retains.
17: 
18: ## Optimize For Human Attention And Direction
19: 
20: Owner decision, accepted 2026-09-19: treat human attention and direction as the
21: scarce resources in agent-assisted development. RelayView's objective is to turn
22: human intent into verified, useful outcomes with less supervision and decision
23: overhead. Producing more code is not sufficient evidence of progress toward that
24: objective.
25: 
26: Use clear contracts, deterministic tools, and admitted automated validation and
27: review to handle work that otherwise demands repeated human checking and
28: correction. Preserve human direction over goals, scope, consequential tradeoffs,
29: and acceptance. Make intervention useful: present the decision needed, the
30: relevant evidence, uncertainty, and consequences without requiring the person
31: to reconstruct the execution history. Routine coordination and repeated
32: explanations should not consume attention that the system can conserve.
33: 
34: The existing [automated review workflow](planner-review-rounds.md) and the planned
35: Human Review Brief serve this objective through different responsibilities:
36: automated review can identify defects before Human review, while the brief is
37: intended to organize the exact candidate, checks, unresolved concerns, and
38: decision context for efficient inspection. The brief remains roadmap work;
39: neither mechanism's existence proves a reduction in human effort.
40: 
41: Evaluate active supervision and review time, avoidable interruptions, repeated
42: instructions, decision quality, and subsequent rework alongside coding outcomes,
43: latency, and resource use. Preserve visibility of uncertainty and required
44: acceptance boundaries while reducing burden. The
45: [human-decision hypothesis](../speculative/relayview-theory-of-effectiveness.md#h6-inspectable-evidence-can-improve-human-decisions-if-it-reduces-review-burden)
46: records the expected benefit and evidence limits. This is a product design
47: priority, not a claim that model capability, correctness, or compute constraints
48: have ceased to matter.
49: 
50: ### Design For Sustained Work Between Human Checkpoints
51: 
52: Owner decision, accepted 2026-09-20: design RelayView for long periods of useful
53: work without routine human input, including overnight runs. Preconfiguration
54: enables unattended execution, which serves the broader objective of conserving
55: human attention. This principle applies across Community and Teams.
56: 
57: Owner decision, accepted 2026-10-04: concentrate necessary Human interaction
58: into deliberate checkpoints that unlock the longest safe interval of independent
59: work. Ask foreseeable questions as soon as there is enough evidence to answer
60: them reliably, and collect related questions, setup steps, and requests for new
61: authority into one useful checkpoint. Optimize the number and timing of
62: interruptions as well as total Human effort. Do not ask speculative questions
63: that the workflow can resolve within its existing authority merely to make a
64: checkpoint look complete.
65: 
66: Move foreseeable configuration and authorization decisions before execution.
67: Let users establish task direction, acceptance criteria, supported capabilities,
68: dependency sources, external-service access, credential bindings, and resource
69: limits upfront. Within that configured authority, design routine acquisition,
70: builds, tests, coordination, and bounded recovery to proceed without repeated
71: user confirmation. Surface detectable missing prerequisites before a run so
72: users can resolve them while preparing the work.
73: 
74: An agent-ready assignment has no known unresolved consequential choice that
75: would predictably stop implementation. Task preparation should expose such
76: choices while a Human is already defining the work; readiness does not promise
77: that unexpected questions will never arise. Collaborative task preparation and
78: unattended implementation are separate interactions. Their overlap lets a Human
79: shape future tasks while ready tasks continue through owner-controlled roles.
80: 
81: When execution encounters a consequential decision, missing configuration, or a
82: need for new authority, preserve progress and continue independent authorized
83: work where possible. Before interrupting the Human, examine other foreseeable
84: decisions needed to resume useful work and present the related questions together
85: with their evidence, options, and consequences. Leave a clear account of any
86: remaining blocker; do not invent permission or count blocked verification as
87: passed. Prepare results and verification evidence for human inspection, manual
88: testing, acceptance, and further direction.
89: 
90: The first safe opportunity to interact with an exact implementation candidate
91: is another useful Human checkpoint. Make that candidate inspectable and, where
92: practical, manually testable so the Human can discover defects or differences
93: from their intent before merge. Formal approval still follows the required
94: current verification and review evidence, and applies only to the candidate
95: actually inspected. A changed candidate needs fresh applicable evidence and a
96: fresh Human decision. This checkpoint is part of conserving attention:
97: discovering an intent mismatch before merge avoids a later interruption and
98: repair cycle.
99: 
100: Make the review package especially usable for intermediate changes whose value
101: is not obvious from a visible feature. Explain why the change matters, identify
102: the exact candidate, and separate what current deterministic checks establish
103: from what they cannot assess. A bounded contract with enumerable inputs and
104: outputs may have strong automated coverage and little value in repeating the
105: same calls by hand. Interface clarity, visual layout, discoverability, and fit
106: to Human intent often need direct inspection even when focused browser tests
107: pass; expanding brittle browser assertions cannot exhaust those judgments.
108: 
109: State the remaining Human review need explicitly. When direct exercise can
110: resolve it, give the shortest repeatable setup, action, and expected observation
111: for the exact candidate. When manual testing adds little, say why the automated
112: evidence is a suitable basis for the Human's decision and name its limits; do
113: not create busywork to fill a checklist. When useful manual testing is
114: impractical, explain the constraint without implying that the Human exercised
115: the behavior. Human acceptance remains necessary in every case, and neither
116: automated coverage nor a successful manual check is proof beyond its stated
117: scope.
118: 
119: The [work-between-checkpoints hypothesis](../speculative/relayview-teams-business-plan.md#market-hypotheses-not-decisions-or-established-evidence)
120: illustrates the intended rhythm: refine tasks and set clear directions in the
121: afternoon, let agents work overnight, then manually test, verify, and redirect in
122: the morning. That schedule is an example, not a requirement. Supporting sustained
123: unattended work is accepted design guidance; whether this rhythm reduces total
124: human effort remains a hypothesis, and this principle does not establish that
125: every supporting capability is implemented.
126: 
127: ## Build For The Only Installation That Exists
128: 
129: Owner decision, accepted 2026-09-19: RelayView has no release and no installation
130: other than the development host. Do not add compatibility for earlier versions of
131: this project's own code. When a change alters a contract, change it, and require
132: the older participant to be rebuilt or relaunched.
133: 
134: Distinguish durable artifacts from live participants, because the project's
135: genuine care about history is what makes this mistake easy. Sessions, events,
136: commands, plans, candidates, and audit records are evidence. They must remain
137: readable with their original semantics, and reinterpreting them would falsify the
138: record. That is history integrity, not backward compatibility, and this heuristic
139: does not weaken it.
140: 
141: Everything a running process holds may change outright: protocol shapes, tool
142: schemas, extension code, prompts, configuration, and any read model that can be
143: rebuilt from durable records.
144: 
145: Apply it as follows. When a change tempts you to add a compatibility path, name
146: the artifact that requires it. If it is a durable record, keep the record
147: readable and say so in the contract. If it is a running process, the answer is
148: to relaunch it. If it is a deployment that does not exist, do not write the
149: code. Symptoms worth catching in review: an alias normalizing a superseded
150: name, an operation accepting two input shapes, a branch keyed on a build that
151: only ever ran here, a migration for data no installation holds, and failure
152: text explaining a shape nothing sends.
153: 
154: Revisit this heuristic when a first release exists. Until then the cost is
155: concrete and recurring: every compatibility seam must be reconsidered by every
156: later change that touches the same contract.
157: 
158: ## Use The Right Tool For The Job
159: 
160: Owner decision, accepted 2026-09-19: choose a mechanism because it fits the
161: required capability and constraints. Evaluate correctness, coverage, reliability,
162: authority, integration fit, and total execution and maintenance cost. Familiarity,
163: availability, or an agent's ability to attempt the work is insufficient by itself.
164: 
165: The [deterministic-systems preference](#prefer-deterministic-systems-wherever-they-can-do-the-work)
166: is RelayView's concrete application of this general maxim: consider integration
167: with existing software, then internal deterministic solutions, then agentic
168: solutions for the remaining work. The maxim explains that ordering rather than
169: replacing it with an unconstrained choice. Apply it to each part of a capability;
170: a combination of mechanisms may fit the job best. Record the concrete limitation
171: or evidence that justifies departing from the default.
172: 
173: ## Treat Agents As Contractors Working Against Verifiable Contracts
174: 
175: Owner decision, accepted 2026-09-19: treat agents as untrusted contractors with
176: clear assignments and verifiable acceptance criteria. Here, untrusted describes
177: an authority boundary, not an assumption of dishonesty. Agents can misunderstand
178: requirements, overlook defects, or sincerely report completion before the work
179: satisfies its contract.
180: 
181: Give an agent a clear contract for what done means: the intended outcome, scope,
182: constraints, and observable acceptance criteria. Treat its completion report as
183: a submitted candidate for validation. Check the exact version it reports against
184: that contract using attributable evidence, and return concrete unmet requirements
185: through the admitted feedback and correction workflow. Changed candidates need
186: current evidence; a report or approval for an earlier version cannot establish
187: that a later version meets the contract.
188: 
189: Use the [deterministic-systems default](#prefer-deterministic-systems-wherever-they-can-do-the-work)
190: to perform checks wherever suitable tools exist, with agent review for remaining
191: context-sensitive judgments. Evaluate whether the checks cover the intended
192: behavior: successful execution of inadequate checks does not establish contract
193: satisfaction. Make requirement changes explicit rather than silently relaxing
194: the contract to fit the submitted work. Keep agent claims, observed validation,
195: review judgments, and Human acceptance distinct.
196: 
197: This principle explains the separation between
198: [implementation reports](implementer-implementation-reports.md),
199: [validation evidence](repository-validation-manifest.md), and

1: # Current Orchestration Architecture
2: 
3: ## Scope
4: 
5: This document describes the behavior implemented by the current TypeScript scaffold. Proposed multi-agent tracking and control behavior is documented separately in [../speculative/multi-agent-observability-and-control.md](../speculative/multi-agent-observability-and-control.md).
6: 
7: The bounded SQLite backup-retention contract is documented in [tracked task storage and recovery](tracked-task-storage-and-recovery.md). Startup conservatively adopts verified historical automatic snapshots, protects the exact recorded recovery point, prunes only revalidated redundant bundles, and exposes bounded path-free status plus an owner-local dry-run plan. Automatic creation and historical cleanup share the same deterministic planner and crash-safe mutation boundary.
8: 
9: Cross-cutting default decision rules live in [Architecture Heuristics](architecture-heuristics.md). They guide new designs but do not themselves claim that behavior is implemented.
10: The [task archive aggregate storage](task-archive-storage.md) persists a
11: role-neutral task retirement checkpoint, bounded API read projections, and
12: authenticated `task.archive` and `task.abandon` commands. Client controls and
13: navigation views remain proposed.
14: The [successor task lifecycle core](successor-task-lifecycle.md) persists an
15: internal merge-gated state machine and exact terminal release proof; its
16: provider/local-Git integration and public Human-review controls remain proposed.
17: The [external CI adapter boundary](external-ci-adapter.md) stores revisioned
18: project bindings and provides owner-private Gitea Actions observation for the
19: internal version-2 validation evidence contract.
20: The [remote hosting adapter boundary](remote-hosting-adapter.md) defines internal
21: repository/ref identity, Gitea observation, and guarded publication semantics;
22: revisioned owner bindings and sanitized client configuration are connected,
23: and owner-controlled publication verifies the exact candidate through a
24: durable intent.
25: The [pull-request adapter boundary](pull-request-adapter.md) defines separate
26: project admission, authenticated Gitea PR and review observation, a
27: policy-required draft effect, and exact-head internal merge recovery.
28: Agent instruction authoring follows the accepted default of
29: [positive action language](architecture-heuristics.md#use-positive-action-language-for-agent-instructions).
30: Authorization and disclosure restrictions follow
31: [external enforcement boundaries](architecture-heuristics.md#enforce-prohibitions-outside-the-agent),
32: independently of model compliance with prompt prohibitions.
33: Tool-call contracts follow
34: [minimized required model transcription](architecture-heuristics.md#minimize-required-model-transcription),
35: resolving owner-held canonical fields from storage instead of requiring the
36: model to reproduce them.
37: 
38: ## Focused Chat And Agent Publications
39: 
40: New focused Chat sessions use the [durable status fallback](focused-chat-status-fallback.md): natural status publications reset a tiered owner timer, and an owner request enters only an already-running Pi model boundary. Timers cannot wake agents or create Human review influence.
41: 
42: Focused Chat provides a retained-history focused-conversation projection and
43: route-addressable Implementer Chat. New task-bound Planner, Implementer, and
44: Reviewer Chat use an owner-mediated, non-interrupting inbox and the private
45: `publish_focused_chat_message` tool rather than transcript inference. Exact

1: # Testing Strategy
2: 
3: ## Purpose
4: 
5: RelayView uses a layered testing strategy shaped like a testing pyramid. Most
6: behavior should be verified by deterministic unit and bounded-integration tests.
7: Progressively smaller suites exercise the built browser, the assembled production
8: workflow, and finally real model-provider behavior.
9: 
10: This document defines the responsibility of each layer and the defaults for
11: placing new coverage. It intentionally does not prescribe fixed test counts or
12: ratios. The important invariant is that most behavioral coverage remains below
13: the browser and real-provider layers, while a small number of higher-level tests
14: prove that the boundaries compose correctly.
15: 
16: Tests are specification artifacts. A behavioral change is incomplete until the
17: appropriate layer verifies its success path, important failures, recovery or
18: state transitions, and externally visible contract.
19: 
20: ## Layers
21: 
22: | Layer | Primary commands | Responsibility | Default characteristics |
23: | --- | --- | --- | --- |
24: | Unit and bounded integration | `npm test` | Domain logic, state machines, storage, API and protocol contracts, security boundaries, adapters, and focused process interactions | Numerous, deterministic, isolated, and as fast as the boundary permits |
25: | Browser integration | `npm run test:browser` | Built Lit UI behavior, routing, component contracts, owner-client integration, accessibility-relevant controls, responsive layout, and large-data behavior | Fewer scenarios using controlled fixtures; assertions focus on behavior and rendered state |
26: | Seeded production showcase | `npm run test:showcase` | Production browser, owner API, durable store, event path, supervisor, and Git-status presentation with representative pre-populated state | Small deterministic suite for assembled evidence surfaces and stable visual review |
27: | Empty-state production workflow | `npm run test:workflow` | Public New Task submission through planner finalization, automatic implementation handoff, validation, Git isolation, session control, restart/recovery, and typed failure behavior | Very small deterministic end-to-end suite using Pi-compatible fake processes and real local infrastructure boundaries |
28: | Real-profile smoke | Manifest-backed workflow smoke and documented admission checks | Actual Pi and model-provider usability, credential delivery, model assignment, tool loops, and a real repository edit | Narrow, explicit, potentially costly, and run only when the affected provider or production boundary requires it |
29: 
30: The first layer is not required to consist only of pure in-memory unit tests.
31: SQLite, filesystem, subprocess, and assembled-service tests belong there when
32: those dependencies are the smallest useful boundary for the behavior. Keep each
33: test focused and deterministic, and avoid promoting coverage to Playwright merely
34: because the implementation crosses modules.
35: 
36: ## Choosing A Layer
37: 
38: Place a regression at the lowest layer that can faithfully prove the behavior:
39: 
40: 1. Prefer a focused Vitest test for logic, persistence, protocol, state, failure,
41:    recovery, and security invariants.
42: 2. Add browser integration coverage when correctness depends on rendering,
43:    browser events, focus, responsive layout, accessibility semantics, routing,
44:    or the browser-facing client contract.
45: 3. Extend a production-path workflow scenario only when the risk is in the
46:    composition of owner, store, events, process supervision, Git, private tools,
47:    and browser behavior. Prefer extending an existing scenario over adding a new
48:    full lifecycle when that preserves fault isolation and readability.
49: 4. Require a real-profile smoke only when deterministic substitutes cannot prove
50:    provider compatibility, credentials, model assignment, or actual model/tool
51:    behavior.
52: 
53: Higher-level coverage complements rather than replaces lower-level coverage. A
54: workflow regression should normally have focused tests for its important domain
55: and failure rules, while the workflow test proves that those rules remain wired
56: together through production boundaries.
57: 
58: ## Determinism And Isolation
59: 
60: The default automated suites must not depend on public network access, provider
61: availability, production credentials, or nondeterministic model output. Use
62: controlled clocks, fixtures, disposable repositories and databases, and
63: Pi-compatible fake processes as appropriate. Tests must not read or retain
64: credentials, private provider diagnostics, or unrelated host state.
65: 
66: Process-backed tests remain part of the normal Vitest layer but must have bounded
67: startup, shutdown, output, and failure behavior. The standard `npm test` command
68: caps Vitest at four workers because greater file concurrency reproducibly caused
69: unrelated process-backed failures; see
70: [Source Layout And Retrieval Evidence](../historical/issue-259-source-layout-evidence.md).
71: 
72: Test files importing `src/api/api-test-fixtures.ts` use a 30-second default
73: through Vitest's file-local runtime configuration. These bounded integration
74: suites include Git, SQLite, HTTP schema setup, workflow execution, and shutdown.
75: <!-- keep-issue-ref: verification-run — the 30-second budget's only support is these two identified measurement runs -->
76: Two measurements support that budget. During #402 acceptance, seven cases across
77: benchmark, workflow, HTTP client, and task-memory suites exceeded the generic
78: five-second default; all completed their assertions in roughly 4.7–6.3 seconds in
79: isolated diagnostics. During #516 acceptance, a cold multi-version API workflow
80: measured 16.5 seconds: its first attachment, snapshot, and task-detail requests
81: consumed 4.2, 2.2, and 7.7 seconds respectively, while later requests to those
82: routes completed in milliseconds.
83: 
84: Keep the budget at the shared fixture boundary rather than adding overrides as
85: individual cases cross that default. The shared budget covers that bounded setup
86: under the existing four-worker gate, and the affected projection and lifecycle
87: scenarios use it rather than per-case 10- or 15-second limits. It relaxes no
88: behavior assertion or owner operation deadline. Other suites retain Vitest's
89: default, and explicit test budgets, operation deadlines, and assertions are
90: unchanged.
91: 
92: Gitea integration cost is verified in the same layer. Deterministic scenarios
93: pin each operation's provider requests, response bytes, and broker activations
94: as exact budgets, assert the operation's result alongside them, and hold local
95: compute only to a generous ceiling, never to a live-latency threshold.
96: [Gitea operation cost budgets](gitea-operation-cost-budgets.md) owns the
97: scenarios, the focused commands, and the explicit budget-update procedure.
98: 
99: ## Browser Assertions And Visual Evidence
100: 
101: Playwright tests assert behavior and rendered-state contracts in code. Named
102: screenshots supplement those assertions with evidence for layout and presentation
103: qualities that are difficult to reduce to stable DOM checks.
104: 
105: Screenshots are currently manual visual-review artifacts, not golden-image
106: snapshots. Do not treat screenshot capture alone as a passing assertion. The
107: reviewer must inspect retained PNGs at original resolution for clipping, overlap,
108: overflow, spacing, misleading state, contradictory status, and unreadable long
109: content, then record defects or explicitly record that none were found. Screenshot
110: artifacts remain ignored by Git.
111: 
112: The empty-state workflow suite captures every asserted workflow state and checks
113: horizontal viewport overflow before capture. The exact procedure and review
114: checklist live in
115: [First Production Browser Workflow Verification](simple-workflow-verification.md).
116: The seeded showcase and accessible-screen inventory are documented in
117: [Live UI Showcase](live-ui-showcase.md). Focused browser regressions and their
118: named visual artifacts are documented in
119: [Browser Task And Session UI](browser-task-session-ui.md).
120: 
121: ## Sustained Browser Streaming
122: 
123: The production workflow replay establishes an explicit earlier transcript reader
124: position before exercising **Jump to latest**; it does not assume that streaming
125: or initial history hydration has incidentally disabled follow-latest. On initial
126: task navigation and after owner restart it waits for the requested task-detail
127: response before checking its rendered cards; cold owner response latency is recorded separately from streaming
128: input responsiveness.
129:

3: ## Purpose

13: the browser and real-provider layers, while a small number of higher-level tests

17: appropriate layer verifies its success path, important failures, recovery or
18: state transitions, and externally visible contract.

22: | Layer | Primary commands | Responsibility | Default characteristics |
23: | --- | --- | --- | --- |
24: | Unit and bounded integration | `npm test` | Domain logic, state machines, storage, API and protocol contracts, security boundaries, adapters, and focused process interactions | Numerous, deterministic, isolated, and as fast as the boundary permits |
25: | Browser integration | `npm run test:browser` | Built Lit UI behavior, routing, component contracts, owner-client integration, accessibility-relevant controls, responsive layout, and large-data behavior | Fewer scenarios using controlled fixtures; assertions focus on behavior and rendered state |
26: | Seeded production showcase | `npm run test:showcase` | Production browser, owner API, durable store, event path, supervisor, and Git-status presentation with representative pre-populated state | Small deterministic suite for assembled evidence surfaces and stable visual review |
27: | Empty-state production workflow | `npm run test:workflow` | Public New Task submission through planner finalization, automatic implementation handoff, validation, Git isolation, session control, restart/recovery, and typed failure behavior | Very small deterministic end-to-end suite using Pi-compatible fake processes and real local infrastructure boundaries |
28: | Real-profile smoke | Manifest-backed workflow smoke and documented admission checks | Actual Pi and model-provider usability, credential delivery, model assignment, tool loops, and a real repository edit | Narrow, explicit, potentially costly, and run only when the affected provider or production boundary requires it |

30: The first layer is not required to consist only of pure in-memory unit tests.
31: SQLite, filesystem, subprocess, and assembled-service tests belong there when
32: those dependencies are the smallest useful boundary for the behavior. Keep each
33: test focused and deterministic, and avoid promoting coverage to Playwright merely
34: because the implementation crosses modules.

36: ## Choosing A Layer

48:    full lifecycle when that preserves fault isolation and readability.

50:    provider compatibility, credentials, model assignment, or actual model/tool
51:    behavior.

54: workflow regression should normally have focused tests for its important domain

56: together through production boundaries.

59: 
60: The default automated suites must not depend on public network access, provider
61: availability, production credentials, or nondeterministic model output. Use
62: controlled clocks, fixtures, disposable repositories and databases, and
63: Pi-compatible fake processes as appropriate. Tests must not read or retain
64: credentials, private provider diagnostics, or unrelated host state.

1: # MCP Integration Placement — Proposed Design
2: 
3: **Status:** Speculative. RelayView has not selected an external MCP server, approved
4: general user-configured MCP servers, or committed to shipping an MCP client. This
5: document preserves the analysis from [issue #191](https://tea.kyle-merritt.com/anodyine/relayview/issues/191)
6: for a future concrete integration decision. It does not grant new runtime authority.
7: 
8: ## Question and working conclusion
9: 
10: If RelayView connects to an external MCP server, where should that connection
11: sit? MCP describes how a client discovers and invokes server capabilities. It
12: does not define RelayView's work-tracker, validation, design-system, or research
13: contract, and a server's catalog does not grant an agent permission to use it.
14: The **working conclusion** is to treat MCP as a possible transport for an
15: admitted capability, rather than as a domain module or an authority source.
16: 
17: There are two plausible narrow paths. An owner-managed provider adapter could
18: use MCP behind a domain-specific interface when an external operation affects
19: workflow state. An owner-assigned Pi role could receive selected read-only
20: capabilities after explicit admission. Neither path implies a marketplace or
21: arbitrary production server configuration. Whether either path is worth building
22: remains open.
23: 
24: RelayView already publishes a [bounded research MCP server](../authoritative/research-mcp.md)
25: for other native clients. That is the opposite direction from connecting its
26: production agents to external MCP servers.
27: 
28: ## Vocabulary and protocol evidence
29: 
30: - **Integration transport:** MCP framing, discovery, and invocation between a
31:   client and provider. It does not define provider identity, effect semantics,
32:   or trust.
33: - **Domain/provider contract:** The typed operation, scope, authority, result,
34:   and recovery contract RelayView applies to a work tracker, validation system,
35:   design system, or research source. An adapter could use MCP privately to
36:   fulfill one such contract.
37: - **Runtime capability:** A Pi tool or resource exposed to a specific agent
38:   role after owner admission. A server advertising a tool does not grant it.
39: - **Supporting context:** An MCP resource or prompt treated as attributed
40:   external content. It is not an owner role prompt or a skill assignment.
41: 
42: This assessment uses the official [MCP specification 2026-07-28](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic)
43: as a dated reference, not a selected implementation target. The existing
44: research server supports earlier revisions, as its current contract records.
45: The specification separates tools, resources, and prompts. Tools are invocable
46: operations and may read or mutate. Resources expose content by URI or template.
47: Prompts are server-supplied templates that may contain instructions. The
48: [tool specification](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/server/tools)
49: says tool annotations are untrusted unless the server is trusted; hints such as
50: `readOnlyHint` and `idempotentHint` cannot substitute for owner policy. The
51: [versioning](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic/versioning)
52: and [authorization](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic/authorization)
53: contracts inform the options below. A future implementation would need to
54: recheck the then-current specification and negotiate a version supported by
55: its chosen client and server.
56: 
57: ## Placement options
58: 
59: | Placement | Authority and credentials | Portability and negotiation | Observation, approval, and failure isolation | Assessment |
60: | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
61: | Pi connects directly | Pi would hold or reach a server credential. A server catalog could bypass owner effect admission unless every call passes an enforced gate. | Pi-specific discovery and exposure; the owner would still need to pin identity, version, schema, and role scope. | Pi history alone cannot prove an external effect or recover an uncertain mutation. | Plausible only for explicitly admitted read-only operations after confinement is verified. Direct mutating access conflicts with current owner-effect boundaries. |
62: | Owner offers a generic MCP proxy | The owner could hold credentials, but a generic proxy could expose arbitrary methods as agent tools. | Reusable transport plumbing; every method still needs a domain contract. | Central logs and cancellation are possible, but a proxy alone does not establish provider concurrency or effect truth. | No concrete use case currently justifies a general agent-facing proxy. |
63: | Owner-managed domain adapter uses MCP internally | The owner retains a scoped credential and checks domain operation, role, project, and policy before calling the server. | A provider could change transport without changing the owner-facing domain contract; the adapter would pin protocol and schema mapping. | The owner can record intent, observe the provider result, and reconcile ambiguous outcomes through provider-native mechanisms. | Strongest candidate for workflow-relevant writes, if a chosen provider benefits from MCP. |
64: | MCP resources or prompts supply context | No authority transfers. An assigned role would receive attributed content only. | Potentially portable, subject to bounds and provenance. | Server text, links, and templates remain untrusted; required context failure must be visible. | Requires a separate context-admission decision. |
65: 
66: This assessment builds on [ADR 0020](../authoritative/adr/0020-keep-agent-skills-within-owner-controlled-roles.md)
67: and [ADR 0021](../authoritative/adr/0021-keep-workflow-effects-in-owner-managed-integrations.md).
68: Those accepted decisions already keep skills inside assigned roles and promised
69: workflow effects in owner-managed operations. MCP by itself does not solve a
70: race between a tool or skill writing an issue, triggering CI, merging code, or
71: reporting validation while the owner is making a related decision.
72: 
73: ## Illustrative uses, not selected integrations
74: 
75: - **Work tracker:** An adapter might map `issue.read` and `comment.add` to one
76:   configured MCP server. The owner would still resolve the exact work item,
77:   apply role and project policy, use provider-native concurrency where
78:   available, and check an uncertain write before retrying. A server's
79:   `create_issue` advertisement would not authorize a planner to create issues.
80: - **External validation:** An adapter might dispatch or observe a CI run over
81:   MCP. Server text saying “passed” would not become validation evidence without
82:   authenticated correlation to the exact repository, candidate revision,
83:   workflow, run, and attempt.
84: - **Design system:** An assigned role might read bounded component metadata.
85:   Editing designs or downloading assets would require separate scope and policy.
86: - **Search/research:** A read-only MCP service might return bounded, attributed
87:   results. It would not replace the production research broker's network and
88:   credential boundary merely because it returns search text.
89: 
90: No provider in these examples has been chosen for implementation.
91: 
92: ## Open product decisions
93: 
94: - Is there a specific external service whose MCP endpoint offers a useful
95:   capability that RelayView cannot already obtain well through its current
96:   adapter or direct API?
97: - Should operators be able to configure selected external servers, or should
98:   RelayView ship only maintained provider integrations? General user-configured
99:   server admission has no approval today.
100: - Is read-only tool search worth its admission and context complexity for that
101:   service? Its quality, latency, and resource tradeoffs need an owner ablation
102:   decision before the implementation shape is fixed.
103: - Which role, project scope, credential, and consent model would the selected
104:   operation actually need? A design for every possible server would be broader
105:   than the present evidence supports.
106: 
107: ## Candidate admission criteria if an integration is chosen
108: 
109: These are proposed acceptance criteria, not claims about an implemented general
110: MCP client. A concrete card should keep only the requirements its selected
111: operation needs and preserve the existing owner safety invariants.
112: 
113: 1. **Admit a bounded server and operation set.** Record an owner-assigned server
114:    ID, trusted executable or endpoint, project and role scope, allowed
115:    operations, credential source and scopes, protocol revisions, and required
116:    capabilities. Remote OAuth consent to connect is distinct from approval of
117:    a particular effect and from Human acceptance of completed work. Credentials
118:    stay outside model arguments and results.
119: 2. **Freeze discoverable authority.** Validate paginated catalogs and schemas,
120:    namespace by owner-assigned server ID plus tool name, and bind the admitted
121:    set to a session or explicit generation. A list or schema change should not
122:    silently expand tools. Search or progressive disclosure may narrow what the
123:    model sees, but cannot enlarge the admitted set. Reopen and restart must
124:    verify the same identity or fail closed.
125: 3. **Bound each call and result.** Check role, project, operation, argument
126:    schema, result size, deadline, and credential scope. Treat descriptions,
127:    resources, prompts, and returned text as untrusted data. Bound pages,
128:    bytes, images, redirects, and retries; redact secrets from model-visible
129:    output and logs. Client-side sampling, elicitation, and roots would need
130:    separate admission because they let a server request additional model,
131:    user, or filesystem interaction.
132: 4. **Give writes an effect contract.** An owner-mediated mutation needs a
133:    precondition, provider-native concurrency or idempotency, a stable action
134:    identity, audit record, authenticated observation, and recovery for timeout,
135:    cancellation, disconnect, and restart. Cancellation does not prove that a
136:    provider did nothing. Never blindly retry an uncertain non-idempotent call;
137:    reconcile out-of-band changes against the owner milestone.
138: 5. **Keep trust boundaries explicit.** Server annotations are hints, not
139:    authorization. Server instructions and OAuth pages cannot change role
140:    authority, evidence, artifact identity, hidden-score isolation, or Human
141:    acceptance. Existing credential and egress confinement remains mandatory.
142: 
143: ## Pi compatibility and discovery
144: 
145: RelayView currently admits Pi CLI/TUI 0.85.0 through its
146: [compatibility manifest](../../compatibility/pi-compatibility.json). The
147: installed 0.85.0 package README says “No MCP”; production roles do not have
148: general MCP discovery. Upstream Pi's [moving MCP documentation](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/main/packages/coding-agent/docs/mcp.md)
149: describes later native registration, namespacing, exposure modes, resources,
150: and tool search. That documentation shows a possible route, not compatibility
151: evidence for RelayView's admitted version. A future direct-runtime proposal
152: would need a pinned Pi release and real checks for tool-call interception,
153: indirect calls, cancellation, restart, and result projection. Pi would still
154: own individual session and context-ledger semantics; RelayView would still
155: own workflow admission, policy, and audit.
156: 
157: ## What would justify an accepted decision
158: 
159: Before turning this assessment into an ADR or implementation commitment, choose
160: at least one actual external provider and user workflow. Show why MCP improves
161: that integration over its direct API or an existing owner adapter, what
162: credential and consent model the operator needs, and whether the provider's
163: read/write behavior can satisfy the relevant owner effect contract. Verify a
164: supported client/server protocol tuple and test read-only catalog drift and a
165: fake uncertain mutation where applicable. Decide whether user-configured
166: servers are a product requirement; this assessment makes no such decision.
167: 
168: [Issue #922](https://tea.kyle-merritt.com/anodyine/relayview/issues/922)
169: captures a possible read-only admission and progressive-disclosure slice.
170: [Issue #923](https://tea.kyle-merritt.com/anodyine/relayview/issues/923)
171: captures a possible owner-managed adapter proof. Both remain in triage. Before
172: designing progressive disclosure, the owner must decide whether to compare it
173: with eager disclosure under the existing frozen ablation configuration
174: contract; no flag or paid benchmark is approved by this document.

63: | Owner-managed domain adapter uses MCP internally | The owner retains a scoped credential and checks domain operation, role, project, and policy before calling the server. | A provider could change transport without changing the owner-facing domain contract; the adapter would pin protocol and schema mapping. | The owner can record intent, observe the provider result, and reconcile ambiguous outcomes through provider-native mechanisms. | Strongest candidate for workflow-relevant writes, if a chosen provider benefits from MCP. |
64: | MCP resources or prompts supply context | No authority transfers. An assigned role would receive attributed content only. | Potentially portable, subject to bounds and provenance. | Server text, links, and templates remain untrusted; required context failure must be visible. | Requires a separate context-admission decision. |
65:
